questions.q: Preterm labour is defined as the process of labour beginning at:
questions.exp: PTL = labour process beginning before 37 weeks. (Book p472)

questions.q: The m/c cause of preterm labour and the iatrogenic example given are:
opts: Idiopathic; induction at 34 weeks in severe pre-eclampsia
questions.exp: Idiopathic is m/c; iatrogenic PTL occurs e.g. when labour is induced at 34 weeks in severe pre-eclampsia. (Book p472)

questions.q: The MOST important risk factor for preterm labour is:
questions.exp: Previous preterm labour is the most important risk factor. (Book p472)

questions.q: Uterine overdistension as a PTL risk arises from:
questions.exp: Overdistension from twins or polyhydramnios predisposes to PTL. (Book p472)

questions.q: Bleeding in pregnancy causing PTL is m/c due to:
questions.exp: Abruptio placenta is the m/c bleeding cause linked to PTL. (Book p472)

questions.q: Maternal and fetal stress contributors to PTL listed are:
opts: Maternal: PIH; fetal: uteroplacental insufficiency and IUGR
questions.exp: Maternal stress (PIH) and fetal stress (UPI, IUGR) are listed. (Book p472)

questions.q: Maternal infections linked to PTL (with NO routine screening advised) are:
opts: Asymptomatic bacteriuria and bacterial vaginosis, neither routinely screened
Syphilis and HIV infection, neither routinely screened
Tuberculosis and malaria, neither routinely screened
Chlamydia and gonorrhoea, neither routinely screened
questions.exp: Maternal infections linked to preterm labour for which no routine screening is advised are asymptomatic bacteriuria and bacterial vaginosis. (Book p472)

questions.q: Preventable preterm labour applies to which patients, and what is the IOC tool?
opts: A previous preterm birth or a short cervix; transvaginal sonography is the tool
All primigravid women, screened by transabdominal sonography
Twin pregnancies alone, screened by magnetic resonance imaging
Preterm prelabour rupture alone, monitored with cardiotocography
questions.exp: Prevention is aimed at women with a previous preterm birth or a short cervix, and transvaginal scan is how the cervix is measured. (Book p472)

questions.q: A 'short cervix' on TVS risking PTL is defined as:
questions.exp: Cervical length ≤2.5 cm denotes a short cervix at risk of PTL. (Book p472)

questions.q: As the cervix dilates in preterm labour it becomes shorter (effacement) and its normal 'T' shape changes in which sequence?
questions.exp: The cervical shape changes T → Y → V → U as preterm labour progresses. (Book p472)

questions.q: ACOG recommends cervical length measurement by TVS between which weeks in all women with h/o PTL?
questions.exp: ACOG: TVS cervical length between 16–24 weeks in all with h/o PTL. (Book p472)

questions.q: Precautions during TVS cervical length measurement:
opts: Empty bladder; measure from internal os to external os
Full bladder; measure only the visible part
Lithotomy with coughing; measure external os to vagina
questions.exp: The bladder must be empty and length measured internal-to-external os. (Book p472)

questions.sec: Causes, risks & prediction of preterm birth
questions.q: All of the following are risk factors for spontaneous preterm birth EXCEPT:
opts: A short cervical length in the second trimester
questions.exp: Prior preterm birth, short cervix, multiples, infection and uterine anomalies raise risk; a previous uncomplicated term birth is reassuring. (Book p472)

questions.q: Besides cerclage and progesterone, which lifestyle measure prevents PTL?
questions.exp: Quitting smoking is listed; bed rest, nutrient supplements and routine screening have no role. (Book p473)

questions.q: Cervical circlage surgery requires ALL three of which indications?
opts: Preterm birth history, cervical length 2.5 cm or less on TVS, singleton
Preterm labour history, a twin pregnancy, and a short cervix
A short cervix, vaginal bleeding, and evidence of infection
A previous LSCS, a short cervix, and a singleton pregnancy
questions.exp: Cervical circlage requires all three of: a history of preterm birth, cervical length 2.5 cm or less on TVS, and a singleton pregnancy. (Book p473)

questions.q: Circlage timing and adjunct therapy:
questions.exp: Circlage is done at 14–24 weeks and progesterone is given with it. (Book p473)

questions.q: Indications for progesterone prophylaxis of PTL:
opts: A previous preterm birth, a cervical length of 25 mm or less, and as an adjunct to cervical cerclage
Only in a twin pregnancy, whatever the cervical length or the obstetric history
Only after preterm prelabour rupture of membranes has already occurred
Only when there is vaginal bleeding from placenta previa in the third trimester
questions.exp: Progesterone is given for a previous preterm birth, an incidental short cervix, or alongside cerclage in a classic history. (Book p473)

questions.q: Progesterone regimens listed: hydroxyprogesterone caproate and micronised progesterone.
opts: Hydroxyprogesterone IM weekly from 16-20 weeks to 36 weeks; micronised PV daily
Hydroxyprogesterone IM weekly from 16-20 weeks to 36 weeks; micronised PV weekly
Hydroxyprogesterone orally daily until 20 weeks; micronised IM at 36 weeks
Hydroxyprogesterone as a single IM dose at 12 weeks; no further doses after
questions.exp: The listed progesterone regimens are hydroxyprogesterone caproate IM weekly starting at 16-20 weeks and stopping at 36 weeks, and micronised progesterone per vaginam daily. (Book p473)

questions.q: Progesterone prevents PTL by acting as a:
questions.exp: Its function is smooth muscle relaxation. (Book p473)

questions.q: True or false: progesterone can stop PTL once contractions have started.
opts: False – it is not a tocolytic and cannot stop labour once contractions start
True – it is the first-line tocolytic agent in preterm labour
True – but only when given together with betamethasone
False – but it does reverse cervical effacement completely
questions.exp: False: progesterone is not a tocolytic and cannot prevent preterm labour once contractions have started. (Book p473)

questions.q: Which interventions have NO role in preventing PTL?
opts: Bed rest, nutrient supplementation and routine screening for infection
questions.exp: Bed rest, nutrient supplementation and routine infection screening have no role. (Book p473)

questions.q: Match the preventive measure with its current place — 1) Vaginal progesterone 2) Cervical cerclage 3) Bed rest and hydration … A) Offered when a short cervix is found on ultrasound, even without a previous preterm birth B) Considered with a cervical length below 25 mm and a history of mid-trimester loss or preterm birth C) Widely used but never shown to prevent preterm birth, so not recommended
questions.exp: Progesterone treats the incidental short cervix, cerclage suits the classic history with a short cervix, and bed rest has no proven benefit. (Book p473)

questions.q: Work-up of uterine contractions with cervical length ≤2.5 cm: per speculum to rule out PROM, then P/V examination. Cervical dilatation ≥2 cm means:
questions.exp: Dilatation ≥2 cm = established PTL requiring admission; <2 cm → admit and observe dilatation/effacement. (Book p473)

questions.q: If dilatation is < 2 cm with contractions and a short cervix, the plan is:
opts: Admit and observe dilatation and effacement
questions.exp: Such patients are admitted for observation of dilatation and effacement. (Book p473)

questions.q: The CONVENTIONAL definition of established PTL needs uterine contractions (4 in 20 min / 8 in 60 min) plus any one of:
opts: Contractions plus a cervical length of 2 cm or less, dilatation of 3 cm or more, or a positive fetal fibronectin
Contractions plus cervical dilatation of 1 cm or more and nothing else
Contractions plus a fetal fibronectin of 10 ng per mL or more in cervicovaginal fluid
Contractions plus a Bishop score of 6 or more with a closed cervix
questions.exp: The conventional definition adds an objective marker: a short cervix, advanced dilatation or a positive fibronectin test. (Book p473)

questions.q: Fill up: Preterm labour is regular uterine contractions with progressive cervical change occurring between ______ and ______ weeks of gestation.
questions.exp: The window runs from 20 weeks to 36 weeks and 6 days; before 20 weeks the loss is called an abortion rather than preterm labour. (Book p473)

questions.q: The CURRENT definition of established PTL replaces those add-ons with:
opts: Progressive cervical change, or an initial dilatation of 2 cm or more
A fixed dilatation of 5 cm or more with no further change
A fetal fibronectin of 100 ng per mL or more in cervicovaginal fluid
A cervical length of 1 cm or less and no other supporting feature
questions.exp: The current definition drops the add-on tests and requires progressive change, or dilatation of at least 2 cm at presentation. (Book p474)

questions.q: Fetal fibronectin is a 'glue' present between the fetal membrane and decidua. In cervicovaginal secretions, a positive result between 22–35 weeks indicates:
questions.exp: Between 22–35 weeks fibronectin positivity suggests PTL or PPROM; after 35 weeks it is normal. (Book p474)

questions.q: After how many weeks is fetal fibronectin in cervicovaginal secretions considered NORMAL?
questions.exp: Beyond 35 weeks its presence is normal. (Book p474)

questions.q: Risks increased in the preterm neonate include RDS (due to decreased surfactant), NEC, IVH, hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, infections and:
opts: Cerebral palsy – prevented by MgSO4 neuroprotection
questions.exp: Cerebral palsy risk is countered with neuroprotective MgSO4; RDS/NEC/IVH with corticosteroids. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which neonatal complications of PTL are reduced by corticosteroids?
questions.exp: Steroids accelerate lung maturity and ↓ RDS, NEC and IVH. (Book p474)

questions.q: Corticosteroids in PTL are indicated in:
opts: All cases before 34 weeks, and from 34 weeks once chorioamnionitis and a previous course are excluded
Only below 28 weeks, since later gestation gains nothing
Only between 34 and 37 weeks, where the benefit is greatest
Every case regardless of infection, because the benefit outweighs the risk
questions.exp: Corticosteroids are given before 34 weeks, and in the late preterm window once infection and prior treatment are excluded. (Book p474)

questions.q: Which condition CONTRAINDICATES corticosteroids in PTL?
questions.exp: Chorioamnionitis contraindicates steroid use. (Book p474)

questions.q: The action of antenatal corticosteroids is seen ______ after the first dose, with maximum benefit ______.
questions.exp: Effect appears 48 hours after the first dose, maximal 2–7 days after. (Book p474)

questions.q: Why are repeat courses of antenatal steroids avoided?
questions.exp: Repeat courses are not given as they can cause cerebral palsy. (Book p474)

questions.q: Match steroid regimens: dexamethasone (DOC in India) and betamethasone (DOC worldwide).
opts: Dexamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12-hourly; betamethasone 2 doses of 12 mg 24-hourly
Dexamethasone 2 doses of 12 mg 24-hourly; betamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg 12-hourly
Dexamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12-hourly; betamethasone 4 doses of 6 mg 12-hourly
Both given as a single dose of 12 mg IM, repeated if delivery is delayed
questions.exp: Dexamethasone (DOC in India) is 4 doses of 6 mg IM 12 hours apart; betamethasone (DOC worldwide) is 2 doses of 12 mg 24 hours apart and carries a slightly higher fetal hypoglycaemia risk. (Book p474)

questions.q: The role of tocolytics in PTL and their maximum duration of use:
opts: To allow corticosteroid action; maximum use till 48 hours
questions.exp: Tocolytics buy 48 hours for steroid action. (Book p475)

questions.q: Tocolytics + corticosteroids are recommended in which group, and have NO role in which three groups?
opts: Preterm labour before 34 weeks; no role after 34 weeks, in twins, or with chorioamnionitis
Preterm labour after 34 weeks only, with no role before 34 weeks
Twin pregnancy alone, with no role in singleton pregnancies
Chorioamnionitis alone, since infection shortens the cervix
questions.exp: Tocolysis with steroids is for early preterm labour; it has no place in late preterm labour, twins or infection. (Book p475)

questions.q: The m/c tocolytic used in India and its ACOG window:
questions.exp: Nifedipine is m/c in India with ACOG use at 32–34 weeks. (Book p475)

questions.q: Atosiban, the oxytocin antagonist, is the tocolytic of choice in:
questions.exp: Atosiban is preferred in cardiac disease. (Book p475)

questions.q: Indomethacin as a tocolytic leads to which fetal effects and is restricted by ACOG to:
opts: Oligohydramnios and premature ductus arteriosus closure; <32 weeks
questions.exp: Indomethacin causes oligohydramnios and premature ductal closure; ACOG limits it to <32 weeks. (Book p475)

questions.q: β-agonist tocolytics listed are:
opts: Nifedipine and atosiban, which are calcium and oxytocin antagonists
Indomethacin and sulindac, which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis
Magnesium sulfate and progesterone, which are used for other purposes
questions.exp: The beta-agonist group is terbutaline, salbutamol, ritodrine and isoxsuprine; the others belong to different drug classes. (Book p475)

questions.q: Side effects of β-agonist tocolytics include tremors, hypotension, tachycardia, pulmonary oedema and:
opts: Hyperglycaemia, which is why they are contraindicated in diabetes
Hypoglycaemia, which needs regular monitoring of blood glucose
Bradycardia, which limits the dose that can safely be given
Isolated hypokalaemia, with no other metabolic disturbance
questions.exp: Beta-agonists cause tremor, tachycardia, hypotension, pulmonary oedema and hyperglycaemia, so they are avoided in diabetes. (Book p475)

questions.q: Two 'not a tocolytic' notes: progesterone is not a tocolytic, and MgSO4 is not used as one because:
opts: Its tocolytic effect appears only at 9-10 mg/dL, the same range as its toxicity
It causes persistent fetal tachycardia that masks the signs of fetal distress
It has no effect at all on the myometrium at any dose that can be given
It paradoxically induces labour by increasing local prostaglandin release
questions.exp: Magnesium relaxes myometrium only at levels that are already toxic, so it is used for neuroprotection rather than tocolysis. (Book p475)

questions.q: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks is in established preterm labour with intact membranes. Corticosteroids and magnesium for neuroprotection have been started. Which tocolytic is most appropriate, and for how long?
opts: Nifedipine or an oxytocin antagonist for up to 48 hours, to complete steroids and arrange transfer
No tocolytic at all, since delaying delivery never helps the baby
Indomethacin after 32 weeks, continued for seven days
Ritodrine for two weeks so that she can be managed at home
questions.exp: Tocolysis buys up to 48 hours for steroids and transfer; indomethacin is avoided after 32 weeks because of ductal constriction and oligohydramnios. (Book p475)

questions.q: MgSO4 in PTL is used for its ______ action and is given in all cases of PTL < ______ weeks.
opts: Neuroprotective action (prevents cerebral palsy); given when PTL is under 32 weeks
Tocolytic action (arrests uterine contractions); given when PTL is under 32 weeks
Neuroprotective action (prevents cerebral palsy); given when PTL is over 34 weeks
Tocolytic action (arrests uterine contractions); given when PTL is over 34 weeks
questions.exp: MgSO4 in preterm labour is given for its neuroprotective action (reducing cerebral palsy), and it is given in all cases of PTL before 32 weeks. (Book p476)

questions.q: MgSO4 dosing for neuroprotection in PTL:
questions.exp: Loading 4 g followed by 1 g maintenance. (Book p476)

questions.q: GBS screening in PTL/PPROM is done at presentation; routine screening in all pregnant women is by rectovaginal swab at:
questions.exp: Routine GBS screening is at 35–37 weeks by rectovaginal swab. (Book p476)

questions.q: Antibiotics in PTL are indicated when:
opts: GBS colonisation, intrapartum fever, or ruptured membranes for 18 hours or more
Routinely for every woman in preterm labour, whatever her colonisation status
Only after delivery, once the baby has been born and the cord has been clamped
Only when clinical chorioamnionitis is already established during labour
questions.exp: Intrapartum antibiotics are given for GBS colonisation, intrapartum fever or prolonged rupture, not routinely to everyone. (Book p476)

questions.q: In the PTL summary table, corticosteroids and GBS screening are given in:
opts: Both are listed for early preterm labour and both again for late preterm labour
Only in early preterm labour, since late preterm labour needs neither
Only in late preterm labour, since early delivery is already inevitable
In neither group, since both are given only after 37 completed weeks
questions.exp: In the summary table corticosteroids and GBS screening appear in both the early and the late preterm labour columns. (Book p476)

questions.q: Tocolytics and MgSO4 in the summary table are reserved for:
opts: Early preterm labour only, with magnesium given only below 32 weeks; none in late preterm labour
Late preterm labour only, since early preterm delivery is inevitable
Both groups equally, with the same agents and the same neuroprotection
Only when chorioamnionitis has been confirmed on amniocentesis
questions.exp: Tocolytics and magnesium belong to early preterm labour; neither has a place in late preterm labour. (Book p476)

questions.q: Antibiotics in the PTL summary table are marked:
opts: X in both late and early PTL
questions.exp: Routine antibiotics are not indicated in either group per the summary. (Book p476)

questions.q: Induction of labour in PTL is generally avoided EXCEPT for:
opts: Fetal distress, chorioamnionitis, abruptio placentae and intrauterine death
Maternal request for delivery at 34 weeks without any medical indication
A post-dates pregnancy that has reached 41 weeks with no sign of labour
An uncomplicated twin pregnancy at 36 weeks with intact membranes
questions.exp: Induction is avoided in preterm labour unless continuing the pregnancy is more dangerous than delivering, as with infection or distress. (Book p476)

questions.q: Fill up: Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is given when delivery is anticipated before ______ weeks, using a loading dose of ______ g.
questions.exp: A 4 g loading dose followed by an infusion is given before 32 weeks and reduces the risk and severity of cerebral palsy in survivors. (Book p476)

questions.q: PROM and PPROM are defined as:
opts: PROM – membrane rupture beyond 37 weeks before onset of labour; PPROM – rupture before 37 weeks
PROM – rupture before 37 weeks; PPROM – after 37 weeks
questions.exp: PROM is rupture beyond 37 weeks pre-labour; PPROM is rupture before 37 weeks. (Book p477)

questions.q: Early PPROM and late PPROM span:
opts: Early <34 weeks; late 34 weeks to 36 weeks + 6 days
questions.exp: Early PPROM <34 weeks; late PPROM 34 to 36+6 weeks. (Book p477)

questions.q: Consequences of PROM include PTL within a week, ↑ chorioamnionitis, abruptio placenta, cord prolapse, oligohydramnios and:
questions.exp: RDS is among the listed consequences. (Book p477)

questions.q: Typical presentation of PROM:
opts: Her clothes are soaked and she reports a sudden gush followed by continued leaking
Painless bright-red bleeding with a soft and non-tender uterus
Fever with a rigid tender uterus and offensive-smelling lochia
Reduced fetal movements alone, without any loss of fluid or bleeding
questions.exp: Rupture of membranes presents as a sudden gush with continuing leak; bleeding suggests abruption or previa, and fever suggests infection. (Book p477)

questions.q: On general examination in PROM, fever indicates:
questions.exp: Fever points to chorioamnionitis. (Book p477)

questions.q: Match P/A findings in PROM: ↓ fundal height, ↑ uterine tone with tense tender rigid uterus, uterine tenderness.
questions.exp: ↓ height = oligohydramnios; ↑ tone/tense rigid = abruptio; tenderness = chorioamnionitis. (Book p477)

questions.q: Which examination should be AVOIDED in PROM and why?
questions.exp: Digital P/V examination is avoided due to infection risk. (Book p477)

questions.q: Sterile per speculum examination in PROM assesses:
opts: Cervical dilatation, pooling of liquor, cord prolapse, and a high vaginal swab for culture
Cervical dilatation alone, since the rest is assessed later by ultrasound
Pooling of fluid alone, because a digital examination is still performed afterwards
Fetal presentation alone, since membrane status is decided from the history
questions.exp: A sterile speculum examination avoids introducing infection while assessing dilatation, liquor, cord and taking a swab. (Book p477)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about prelabour rupture of membranes is TRUE?
opts: The earlier the gestation at rupture, the higher the risk of chorioamnionitis, pulmonary hypoplasia and cord prolapse
Rupture of membranes before labour always demands immediate delivery, whatever the gestation
Rupture of membranes at term is labelled prelabour rupture of membranes
Prophylactic antibiotics have no effect on latency and are given only for established infection
questions.exp: At term, rupture before labour is called prelabour rupture (PROM); preterm rupture is PPROM, and antibiotics do prolong latency and reduce infection. (Book p477)

questions.q: Differentiating amniotic fluid from urine relies on:
opts: The ammoniacal smell of urine, and dribbling seen on coughing after the bladder is emptied
The colour of the fluid, which is reliably yellow for urine and clear for liquor
The volume passed, since urine is always lost in a single large gush
The characteristic sweet odour of amniotic fluid on the bed linen
questions.exp: Emptying the bladder with a catheter and then watching for further loss on coughing separates urine from amniotic fluid. (Book p478)

questions.q: The Nitrazine test principle uses pH: amniotic fluid is ______ and vaginal discharge is ______.
questions.exp: Amniotic fluid pH 7.2 (alkaline) vs vaginal discharge pH 3.5 (acidic). (Book p478)

questions.q: On litmus paper, amniotic fluid ______ while vaginal discharge ______.
questions.exp: Blue = alkaline amniotic fluid; yellow = acidic discharge. (Book p478)

questions.q: False-positive Nitrazine tests can be due to:
opts: Blood, semen, bacterial vaginosis, trichomonas infection and meconium
Contamination with urine, which is the only recognised cause
Contamination with the normal saline used for the examination
The cervical mucus plug alone, which is strongly alkaline
questions.exp: Nitrazine turns blue with any alkaline fluid, so blood, semen, infected discharge and meconium all give false positives. (Book p478)

questions.q: The fern test is microscopy of vaginal discharge; a fern-like appearance indicates amniotic fluid because of:
questions.exp: Sodium chloride crystallisation produces the ferning pattern. (Book p478)

questions.q: On USG in PROM you expect:
opts: Reduced amniotic fluid because the membranes have ruptured
Polyhydramnios from accumulation of the leaking fluid
Normal amniotic fluid volume is always seen in these cases
A snowstorm appearance throughout the uterine cavity
questions.exp: On ultrasound in PROM one expects reduced amniotic fluid due to rupture of the membranes. (Book p478)

questions.q: Match the bedside kit tests: the Actim test and the Amnisure test detect:
opts: Actim: placental protein 12, or insulin-like growth factor binding protein-1 — Amnisure: PAMG-1
Actim: PAMG-1 — Amnisure: alpha-fetoprotein in the vaginal fluid
Both tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin in vaginal fluid
Both tests detect fetal fibronectin in cervicovaginal secretions
questions.exp: Actim detects IGFBP-1 (placental protein 12) and Amnisure detects placental alpha microglobulin-1 in vaginal fluid. (Book p478)

questions.q: All of the following help to diagnose rupture of membranes EXCEPT:
opts: Sterile speculum examination showing pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix
Nitrazine or pH testing of vaginal fluid
Ferning of dried vaginal fluid seen under the microscope
questions.exp: Pooling on speculum, an alkaline pH and arborisation (ferning) diagnose rupture; amniotic fluid tests such as AFP belong to other diagnoses. (Book p478)

questions.q: In the PROM/PPROM management table, the MAIN risk in term PROM vs early PPROM is:
questions.exp: Term PROM risks chorioamnionitis; early PPROM adds RDS. (Book p479)

questions.q: Induction of labour is indicated (+) in which column of the PROM table?
opts: Term prelabour rupture only; not in early or late preterm rupture
Early preterm rupture of membranes only, to avoid ascending infection
Late preterm rupture of membranes only, once the lungs are mature
All three groups, since rupture of membranes alone is an indication
questions.exp: Induction is listed only for term prelabour rupture; preterm rupture is managed expectantly unless another indication appears. (Book p479)

questions.q: Corticosteroids and tocolytics in the PROM table: steroids are given in ______ and tocolytics only in ______.
opts: Early and late PPROM; early PPROM
questions.exp: Steroids (+) in both PPROM groups; tocolytics (+) only in early PPROM. (Book p479)

questions.q: MgSO4 in the PROM table is given:
opts: Only in early PPROM when the pregnancy is under 32 weeks
In all cases of PROM, whatever the gestation
Only in late PPROM, that is after 34 weeks
Never in PROM, since tocolysis is contraindicated
questions.exp: In the PROM table, MgSO4 is given only in early PPROM with period of gestation under 32 weeks. (Book p479)

questions.q: GBS prophylaxis in term PROM is given only if:
opts: Membranes ruptured ≥18 hours OR fever ≥100.4°F for 4 hours
Only with positive screening in early PPROM
questions.exp: Term PROM needs prophylaxis only with ROM ≥18 h or intrapartum fever ≥100.4°F for 4 h; both PPROM groups get it. (Book p479)

questions.q: ACOG's GBS screening recommendation is:
opts: 35–37 weeks in all pregnant women by rectovaginal swab
questions.exp: Universal rectovaginal swab at 35–37 weeks. (Book p479)

questions.q: The role of GBS prophylaxis is to prevent:
questions.exp: Prophylaxis prevents early neonatal sepsis. (Book p479)

questions.q: GBS prophylaxis WITHOUT needing screening is indicated for:
opts: A previous infant with GBS sepsis, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, or a positive screening swab
Preterm labour alone, whatever the screening result or the previous obstetric history
Intrapartum fever alone, even with a negative screen and no other risk factor
Rupture of membranes for twelve hours alone, with no other risk factor present
questions.exp: A previous affected infant, bacteriuria in this pregnancy or a positive swab all justify prophylaxis without screening. (Book p479)

questions.q: If GBS screening was NOT done, prophylaxis is still given for:
opts: Preterm labour, preterm rupture, rupture for 18 hours or more, or intrapartum fever
Term labour alone with intact membranes and no other risk factor
An elective caesarean section before labour with the membranes intact
A post-term pregnancy that has gone beyond 41 completed weeks
questions.exp: When the GBS status is unknown, prophylaxis is given on the basis of these clinical risk factors. (Book p479)

questions.q: Timing and DOC for GBS prophylaxis, with alternatives:
opts: Intrapartum benzyl penicillin, with ampicillin or cefazolin and clindamycin if she is penicillin-allergic
Antepartum oral erythromycin given for a week before the expected date of delivery
Postpartum metronidazole started once the placenta has been delivered
Intrapartum gentamicin alone as a single intramuscular injection
questions.exp: Prophylaxis must be intrapartum to clear carriage at delivery: benzyl penicillin, with alternatives for allergy. (Book p479)

questions.q: A woman at 34 weeks with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes is afebrile, with a normal CTG and normal inflammatory markers. What is the management?
opts: Expectant management with antibiotics, corticosteroids and close monitoring, planning delivery around 34-37 weeks
Immediate caesarean section to avoid infection
Induction of labour within twelve hours, whatever the gestation
Discharge home on oral antibiotics with weekly outpatient review
questions.exp: Expectant care with antibiotics and surveillance balances prematurity against infection; delivery is timed by gestation and any sign of infection or compromise. (Book p479)

questions.q: Chorioamnionitis is best described as a:
questions.exp: It is a polymicrobial infection. (Book p480)

questions.q: Presumptive clinical diagnosis of chorioamnionitis requires ruptured membranes + temperature ≥39°C plus any one of:
opts: Fetal tachycardia, a maternal white cell count of 15,000 or more, or pus from the internal os
Maternal bradycardia with a falling blood pressure and cold peripheries
Oligohydramnios with a reduced amniotic fluid index on the ultrasound scan
Meconium-stained liquor with a normal maternal temperature and pulse rate
questions.exp: Presumptive chorioamnionitis is ruptured membranes with fever plus fetal tachycardia, maternal leucocytosis or purulent cervical discharge. (Book p480)

questions.q: Maternal tachycardia and uterine tenderness in chorioamnionitis are:
questions.exp: They are features, not part of the diagnostic criteria. (Book p480)

questions.q: Definitive diagnosis of chorioamnionitis is by:
opts: Amniocentesis with Gram stain, culture and histology of the fetal membranes
Clinical criteria alone, which are sensitive and specific enough on their own
A raised maternal C-reactive protein measured on admission in labour
Ultrasound findings of debris and a thickened placenta
questions.exp: Clinical criteria make a presumptive diagnosis; definitive diagnosis needs amniotic fluid studies and membrane histology. (Book p480)

questions.q: Antibiotic regimen for chorioamnionitis:
questions.exp: Ampicillin with gentamicin is the regimen. (Book p480)

questions.q: Delivery plan in chorioamnionitis:
opts: Induction of labour with vaginal delivery preferred
Wait for spontaneous labour beyond 48 h
questions.exp: Induction and vaginal delivery are preferred. (Book p480)

questions.q: Why is C-section not preferred in chorioamnionitis?
opts: It increases chances of postpartum endometritis
questions.exp: C-section ↑ postpartum endometritis risk; it is reserved for obstetric reasons. (Book p480)

questions.q: The ONLY indication for C-section in chorioamnionitis is an obstetric reason such as contracted pelvis or placenta previa; in that case which drug is added?
questions.exp: Metronidazole is added when C-section is performed. (Book p480)

questions.q: Antibiotics in chorioamnionitis are stopped when:
opts: The patient is afebrile for 24 hours
48 hours after delivery regardless of fever
questions.exp: Afebrile × 24 hours allows stopping antibiotics. (Book p480)

questions.q: Match the feature with its significance in chorioamnionitis — 1) Maternal fever 2) Fetal tachycardia 3) Uterine tenderness with offensive liquor … A) A baseline above 160 bpm, often an early and easily missed fetal sign B) A core temperature of 38 C or more with maternal tachycardia C) Clinical evidence of intrauterine infection requiring delivery and intravenous antibiotics
questions.exp: Maternal fever plus fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness and offensive liquor form the clinical triad that demands delivery and antibiotics. (Book p480)

questions.q: The total normal duration of pregnancy is quoted as:
questions.exp: Normal duration: 9 months + 7 days = 40 weeks = 280 days. (Book p481)

questions.q: Post-term pregnancy is defined as:
opts: 42 weeks or more, that is 294 days or more
40 weeks or more, that is 280 days or more
41 weeks or more, that is 287 days or more
37 weeks or more, that is 259 days or more
questions.exp: Post-term pregnancy is defined as 42 weeks or more (294 days or more). (Book p481)

questions.q: The FIRST step when a history of post-term pregnancy is given:
questions.exp: First review the menstrual history to confirm dates. (Book p481)

questions.q: In post-term pregnancy the amniotic fluid colour and volume at ≥42 weeks are:
questions.exp: Fluid becomes saffron/yellowish-green and volume falls to about 300 ml. (Book p481)

questions.q: Why can the placenta not synthesise estrogen independently?
questions.exp: The placenta lacks 17α-hydroxylase, making estrogen synthesis dependent on fetal adrenals. (Book p481)

questions.q: Order the fetal-placental estrogen pathway for onset of labour.
opts: Fetal adrenal C19 → 17α-hydroxylase → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental sulphatase and aromatase → estrogen → contractility
Placental estrogen → fetal adrenal C19 → 17α-hydroxylase → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental sulphatase → contractility
Fetal adrenal C19 → placental aromatase → DHEA/DHEA-S → 17α-hydroxylase → estrogen → myometrial contractility
Placental sulphatase → fetal adrenal C19 → DHEA/DHEA-S → placental aromatase → estrogen → myometrial relaxation
questions.exp: Fetal adrenal C19 steroids undergo 17α-hydroxylase action to DHEA/DHEA-S, then placental sulphatase and aromatase make estrogen (E1, E2, E3), which raises myometrial contractility. (Book p481)

questions.q: The pathophysiology of post-term pregnancy is:
opts: Falling estrogen reduces myometrial contractility, so labour is hard to start
Rising estrogen makes the labour precipitate and very short
Rising progesterone causes uterine rupture before labour
Falling prostaglandins alone, with normal estrogen levels
questions.exp: Post-term pregnancy is explained by reduced estrogen leading to reduced myometrial contractility, so initiating labour is difficult. (Book p481)

questions.q: Causes of post-term pregnancy listed include:
opts: Anencephaly, placental sulphatase deficiency, fetal demise and fetal Down syndrome
Maternal diabetes, polyhydramnios and an already macrosomic fetus
Cervical incompetence, placenta previa and multiple uterine fibroids
Hyperemesis gravidarum, severe maternal anaemia and Rh isoimmunisation
questions.exp: Post-term pregnancy is linked to an absent or hypoplastic fetal pituitary-adrenal axis and to sulphatase deficiency; maternal diabetes tends to shorten gestation. (Book p481)

questions.q: Macrosomia in post-term pregnancy by Indian guidelines means fetal weight:
questions.exp: Indian guidelines define macrosomia as ≥4.0 kg. (Book p481)

questions.q: Oligohydramnios in post-term pregnancy leads to:
opts: Less space, so cord compression with variable decelerations, then fetal distress and meconium passage
Hydramnios with cord prolapse once the membranes rupture spontaneously in labour
Uterine overdistension leading to rupture of a previously scarred uterus
An entirely normal cardiotocograph, since liquor volume does not affect the trace
questions.exp: Falling liquor in a post-term pregnancy compresses the cord, giving variable decelerations, fetal distress and meconium-stained liquor. (Book p481)

questions.q: Placental ageing in post-term pregnancy causes:
opts: Uteroplacental insufficiency, giving late decelerations and fetal distress
Accelerated fetal growth from continued nutrient transfer
An increase in amniotic fluid volume from fetal polyuria
The early spontaneous onset of labour well before term
questions.exp: The ageing placenta fails, producing late decelerations on the CTG and fetal distress in labour; liquor falls rather than rises. (Book p481)

questions.q: Fill up: Post-term pregnancy is defined as a gestation of ______ weeks or more, and the added fetal risk comes mainly from ______.
questions.exp: Beyond 42 weeks the ageing placenta may fail, liquor falls and the risk of meconium, macrosomia and stillbirth rises. (Book p481)

questions.q: ACOG management of post-term pregnancy: termination of pregnancy at ______ by ______.
questions.exp: ACOG advises TOP at ≥41 weeks via induction of labour. (Book p482)

questions.q: Post-term pregnancy is a ______ for VBAC.
questions.exp: It is a relative contraindication to vaginal birth after C-section. (Book p482)

questions.q: Risk factors for macrosomia listed are:
opts: Post-term pregnancy, maternal diabetes, maternal obesity and a male fetus
Maternal anaemia, cigarette smoking during pregnancy and first pregnancy
Pre-eclampsia, placental insufficiency and a female fetus
Maternal hypothyroidism, hyperemesis gravidarum and teenage pregnancy
questions.exp: Macrosomia follows excess substrate (diabetes, obesity, postmaturity) and male sex; smoking and vascular disease cause growth restriction. (Book p482)

questions.q: Complications increased with macrosomia:
opts: Caesarean section, instrumental delivery, prolonged labour and shoulder dystocia
Postpartum haemorrhage alone, with no effect on the mode of delivery
Malpresentation alone, with no increase in operative delivery
Prelabour rupture of membranes alone, with no intrapartum complications
questions.exp: Macrosomia raises the whole spectrum of obstructed labour complications, including shoulder dystocia and operative delivery. (Book p482)

questions.q: The organ LEAST affected by macrosomia is:
questions.exp: The brain is least affected per the note. (Book p482)

questions.q: Best mode of delivery in macrosomia and C-section thresholds:
opts: Vaginal delivery; C-section at 4.5 kg in diabetics or 5.0 kg in non-diabetics
Vaginal delivery; C-section at 4.0 kg in diabetics or 4.5 kg in non-diabetics
Elective C-section for all; no weight threshold is applied in either group
Vaginal delivery only; C-section at 4.5 kg in diabetics and non-diabetics alike
questions.exp: In macrosomia vaginal delivery is the usual mode; caesarean is advised at 4.5 kg in diabetics and at 5.0 kg in non-diabetics. (Book p482)

questions.q: Macrosomia is a ______ contraindication for VBAC.
questions.exp: It is a relative contraindication for VBAC. (Book p482)

questions.q: Best USG method and parameter for estimating fetal weight:
opts: Formulae such as Hadlock or Shepherd, with abdominal circumference the most useful single parameter
Biparietal diameter and femur length measured in the second trimester
Head circumference combined with the placental grade
Three-dimensional volume measurement with the amniotic fluid index
questions.exp: Composite formulae using abdominal circumference estimate fetal weight best, and abdominal circumference is the most sensitive parameter for growth restriction. (Book p482)

questions.q: Johnson's formula for clinical fetal weight estimation is:
opts: (Fundal height in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Fundal height in cm plus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
Fundal height in cm times 155, minus n, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
(Abdominal circumference in cm minus n) times 155, where n is 12 above the spines and 11 below
questions.exp: Johnson's formula subtracts 12 when the head is above the ischial spines and 11 when it is engaged, and multiplies the result by 155. (Book p482)

questions.q: For a valid abdominal circumference measurement, which three structures must be visible?
opts: Umbilical vein, portal sinus (hockey-stick sign) and fetal stomach
questions.exp: The AC plane shows umbilical vein, portal sinus and fetal stomach. (Book p482)

questions.q: Which structures must NOT be visible at the AC measurement plane?
questions.exp: Kidney and cord insertion should be absent from the plane. (Book p482)

questions.sec: ACOG management of post-term pregnancy & macrosomia
questions.q: A 34-year-old with an uncomplicated pregnancy reaches 41 weeks and 3 days. The CTG is normal and the amniotic fluid index is 9 cm. What is the recommended management?
opts: Offer induction of labour between 41 and 42 weeks, with increased fetal surveillance if she chooses to wait
Reassure her and await spontaneous labour until 43 weeks without intervention
Immediate caesarean section, because post-term fetuses never tolerate labour
Admit for daily amniocentesis to test fetal lung maturity
questions.exp: Induction is offered from 41 weeks because perinatal risk falls; membrane sweeping and increased monitoring are options while she waits. (Book p482)

units.title: causes, risks & prediction
units.guide: Identify idiopathic and iatrogenic preterm labour, rank its risk factors and use TVS cervical length with its shape change to predict it. Focus for this checkpoint: PTL: causes, risks & prediction.

units.title: prevention – cerclage & progesterone
units.guide: Apply the three-part cerclage indication, progesterone regimens and the honest limits of progesterone once contractions begin. Focus for this checkpoint: PTL: prevention – cerclage & progesterone.

units.title: diagnosis & definitions → fetal fibronectin & neonatal risks
units.guide: Move from the conventional to the current definition of established PTL, interpret fetal fibronectin by gestational window and link each neonatal risk to its prevention. Focus for this checkpoint: PTL: diagnosis & definitions, PTL: fetal fibronectin & neonatal risks.

units.title: corticosteroids → tocolytics
units.guide: Time steroid courses, avoid repeats, and pick tocolytics by gestation and maternal disease while knowing why MgSO4 and progesterone are not tocolytics. Focus for this checkpoint: PTL: corticosteroids, PTL: tocolytics.

units.title: MgSO4, GBS & antibiotics; summary
units.guide: Give neuroprotective MgSO4 below 32 weeks, screen and prophylax GBS correctly and read the early-versus-late PTL summary grid. Focus for this checkpoint: PTL: MgSO4, GBS & antibiotics; summary.

units.title: definitions & consequences
units.guide: Define PROM and its preterm subtypes, then examine safely with speculum while watching for chorioamnionitis, abruptio and cord prolapse. Focus for this checkpoint: PROM/PPROM: definitions & consequences.

units.title: diagnosis – fluid evaluation
units.guide: Run the bedside and kit tests that prove ruptured membranes: Nitrazine, ferning, ultrasound and the PAMG-1/placental protein assays. Focus for this checkpoint: PROM: diagnosis – fluid evaluation.

units.title: management & GBS prophylaxis
units.guide: Choose induction, steroids, tocolytics and MgSO4 by PROM category and apply GBS screening and intrapartum prophylaxis rules. Focus for this checkpoint: PROM: management & GBS prophylaxis.

units.title: Chorioamnionitis
units.guide: Diagnose chorioamnionitis clinically with the temperature plus one criterion rule, confirm definitively and deliver vaginally with ampicillin-gentamicin. Focus for this checkpoint: Chorioamnionitis.

units.title: overview & pathophysiology
units.guide: Define post-term pregnancy, follow the fetoplacental estrogen pathway to labour onset and trace oligohydramnios to meconium aspiration. Focus for this checkpoint: Post-term pregnancy: overview & pathophysiology.

units.title: ACOG management & macrosomia
units.guide: Induce at 41 weeks per ACOG, weigh the macrosomic fetus by ultrasound and Johnson's formula and apply the C-section weight thresholds. Focus for this checkpoint: Post-term: ACOG management & macrosomia.
